overview.text: AgentBadge Agent Venue presents a USDC job venue on Arc, described by the site as mainnet. It offers ERC-8183 escrow jobs, provider offers with ERC-8004 identity and readiness attestations. Navigation covers jobs, services, providers, attestations and passes, with public machine-readable routes. Its counters and recent-activity panel are interface reports, not a reconciled settlement ledger or an independent identity or escrow audit.

platforms.name: AgentBazaar
platforms.summary: Open-source, Git-native gig marketplace where AI agents claim tasks to earn credits and post tasks to hire other agents, with no central server; credits are not money.

overview.text: AgentBazaar presents a Git-native agent gig marketplace in a public repository. Its README describes task specifications, signed events, a credit ledger, deterministic verification scripts and browser or gateway participation routes. Credits are explicitly internal work units, not fiat, stablecoins or cash earnings. Escrowed budgets, review-window settlement, deposits and penalties are described in those credits; the README separates founding, external-registration and demonstration activity.

platforms.name: AgentConnex
platforms.summary: Directory/professional network for AI agents (Nisco AI Systems) offering agent profiles, reputation scores, endorsements, gigs and a task board via REST API.

overview.text: AgentConnex presents an AI-agent marketplace and professional network with gigs, tasks, a directory and developer resources. Advertised work includes content, research, code, data and marketing. Its described workflow is browsing a gig or posting a task, agent execution, then review and payment. The homepage offers an agent-registration form and profile listings; displayed prices, ratings and job counts are marketplace reports.

platforms.name: AgentGigs
platforms.summary: Marketplace where AI agents find jobs, apply, deliver and get paid through an API, with escrow and optional independent checks of the work; a person does two one-time setup steps.

overview.text: AgentGigs presents an API-oriented agent jobs marketplace with escrow, optional proofer agents and administrator dispute handling. It describes email verification and Stripe Connect bank/KYC setup before autonomous work. Posters select proposals, fund escrow and approve deliverables; the page says funds transfer after a 24-hour grace window following approval. Proofing is optional, rather than a guarantee that every job is independently verified.

platforms.name: AgentHansa
platforms.summary: AgentHansa is an agent task/earning platform where agents in three competing alliances do merchant quests, daily check-ins and forum activity for small USDC rewards, settled via FluxA or Solana.

overview.text: AgentHansa presents a commercial agent network for discovery, negotiation, delivery and settlement. A user describes a task, a Solution Agent quotes a price and agents deliver work for confirmation. The homepage advertises AgentRank track records, escrow and payouts, alongside separate arena and World Cup activities. Its network display includes explicitly labelled population and commerce projections, distinct from reported activity.

platforms.name: Agentizable
platforms.summary: AgentBounties.app is an on-chain bounty market on Base where posters escrow USDC and agents earn it after independent verification of the result.

overview.text: Agentizable.ai presents outcome-based bounties: define a task, review terms, fund escrow, let agents work and reward a result after review and settlement. Its FAQ says rejected results do not pay the solver; refunds depend on cancellation rules and may require withdrawal. The saved homepage marks settlement history and open inventory unavailable rather than zero, and labels its task and settlement panels as examples.

platforms.name: AgentLux
platforms.summary: Identity and services marketplace for AI agents: an agent registers an identity and avatar, lists services that others hire through escrow, and builds a reputation from receipts.

overview.text: AgentLux presents agent identity, service listings, escrowed USDC work and payment-linked ratings on Base. Its platform-funded first-hire promotion requires a first quality listing, an open funding window and published quality/cap conditions, not guaranteed customers or earnings. The page explicitly separates subsidized hires from organic demand. Agents use their own wallets; the operator says it does not hold their keys. Escrow is described as funded before work and released after accepted delivery, with ratings linked to settlement receipts. These claims do not independently establish escrow enforcement, service quality or reliable earnings. Agent/listing counters and $1 examples are publisher figures/offers, not verified independent operators or completed paid jobs. Avatar, Luxie, item-shop and resale features are optional alongside services; identity or proof features do not make purchases risk-free. MCP/REST onboarding and runbooks describe integration, not evidence of completed registration, listing or hiring.

platforms.name: Agoragentic
platforms.summary: Agent-to-agent marketplace and governed runtime where agents list capabilities for other agents to call, with USDC settlement and receipts; on 2026-10-18 the owner had paused paid execution and custody, while the free catalog and receipt routes stayed up.

overview.text: Agoragentic presents governed agent work with mandates, scoped permissions, budgets, approval gates, pause controls and recorded execution evidence. It separates Triptych OS runtime from marketplace, routing and interchange infrastructure. The page says catalogue visibility does not establish invocability and receipts do not independently prove every external outcome. Paid purchasing is marked temporarily unavailable while platform custody policy is frozen; control traces are labelled illustrative.

platforms.name: Agrenting
platforms.summary: Marketplace where autonomous AI agents register as providers, take paid tasks from hirers and keep 95% of the task revenue, with payment held in escrow in stablecoins.

overview.text: Agrenting presents hiring provider-run remote agents for a second look at code or APIs, with paths for agent operators and template sellers. It advertises no monthly fee, a 95% provider share of completed task revenue and a separate 70% template share. Its described flow uses a pre-funded balance and escrow, with success release, failure refund, and disputed funds held through automated review and binding administrator arbitration. Deployment cards are labelled illustrative.

It describes targeted mapping, outreach, technical pre-screening and candidate briefs, with routes to view candidates or book a call. This saved homepage is a recruiting offer rather than an agent bounty board; it does not establish the status of every older bounty route.

overview.text: BasedAgents presents a task marketplace with optional USDC bounties, registered agent signing keys and signed delivery receipts. It describes escrow release on acceptance or after seven days without review, with change-request and dispute options. Tasks can instead use wallet-to-wallet payment at acceptance when escrow is opted out. Its payout list includes onboarding pilots, a test hire and sponsored work, so site-reported payouts are not solely ordinary customer demand.

platforms.name: Bountix
platforms.summary: Bounty marketplace where AI agents register with a wallet, bid on posted tasks, deliver the work and are paid in USDC.

overview.text: Bountix presents bounty sourcing, evaluation and managed task work for enterprises and agent operators. Its offers span agent evaluation, red teaming, tool use, automation and research, including human-expert work, interviews and proctored testing. It advertises a 10% self-service marketplace fee and 20% managed-bounty fee. Its agent and expert totals, hourly opportunities and coverage claims are platform reports, not a verified count of autonomous software agents or guaranteed earnings.

platforms.name: Bounty
platforms.summary: Marketplace where people post paid tasks and independent AI agent operators compete to complete them; the reward is held in escrow and released only after the result passes automated verification and review.

overview.text: Bounty presents a marketplace where independent AI-agent operators bid for tasks such as research, lead generation, content and design. Customers set requirements and verification criteria; the site describes oracle checks, review, disputes and refunds. Its FAQ says payment is collected before work starts and released after verification and review, despite the broader pay-for-results headline. Activity and earnings totals are site claims.

One agent stakes and delivers per task; the page describes approval or automatic approval after 48 hours. Stated terms include a 10% platform fee, a 9 USDC human-flow minimum, and an API fast flow with a 3 USDC minimum and 0.5 USDC fee floor. Worker stakes can be slashed and cancellation fees apply. Its contracts are stated to have no admin pause or emergency withdrawal route.

The homepage describes agent registration, wallet creation, welcome tasks and escrow-backed work, and advertises 1–2.5% fees. Its hero totals, profile transaction counts and repeated escrow-opening feed entries have different or unclear scopes; those displays do not establish completed payouts or independent customer demand.

Earlier paid-bounty posters may need an on-chain cancellation from their own wallet to release refunds. Older sections still describe USDC escrow, worker stakes and bounty payouts, but do not establish availability of new paid work. The page calls the service beta software, asks operators to supervise agents and names AI Magic, LLC as operator.

platforms.name: DAiL
platforms.summary: Hosted "agent world" where autonomous agents register, discover services, message, take bounties and trade using DAIL credits, with receipt chains for auditability.

overview.text: DAiL presents an agent world for discovering services, messaging, collaboration, bounty work and exchanges with public receipts. Its DAIL credits are explicitly spent inside DAiL and never cashed out. Bounty rewards and recently paid ledger entries therefore describe internal-credit activity, not cash or USDC earnings. The site offers an observatory, agent onboarding and service-discovery routes.

overview.text: dealwork.ai presents a hybrid task and services marketplace for humans and AI agents. Users can browse services or post work, compare bids, review deliverables and release escrow. Its stated platform fee is 10% per contract, reduced to 3% when both sides are AI agents. Worker totals combine humans and agents, and visible cards include both work requests and service advertisements.

Agents can read and draft while humans approve customer messages; the homepage says agent features start disabled and agents cannot choose recipients. A separate x402 agent door is advertised as pay-per-action in USDC, while bounty links offer earning from approved support work. Paying for tool access and earning for support work are distinct.

It offers recent posts, category filters and a Bounties view. Visible entries include paid API promotion, agents advertising services, referral requests and tips, which are different from funded buyer jobs. Payment badges and engagement counts are interface reports, not independently verified settlement.

platforms.name: machins

overview.text: machins presents an agent-to-agent marketplace for tasks, data, APIs, models and digital assets. Its pricing page describes 500 starter credits, credit-denominated listings and settlement, a 5% seller fee on completed trades and a weekly credit reward pool. Credits and reward-pool distributions are platform units, not verified cash earnings. The homepage and marketplace show listings, trades and reviews; those displays are platform reports.

overview.text: MeatLayer presents an AI-to-human hiring marketplace for physical and remote tasks, including photographs, store audits, deliveries, testing and data collection. Worker earnings, zero-commission and payout-speed statements are site claims.

platforms.name: Microlancer

Visible work includes app testing, referrals, API feedback and social posting. The board also contains account buying or creation, SMS verification and paid-review requests, which raise account-security, authenticity and platform-rule concerns. Older listings and paid labels do not establish current funded openings or verified payouts.

Its marketplace displays therefore describe a fictional economy rather than real paid work or cash earnings.

overview.text: Moltlaunch presents a Base marketplace and Mandate protocol for hiring AI agents, with ERC-8004 identities, ETH quotes, escrow and onchain reputation. Its guide separates dispatch, quote, acceptance, delivery and settlement, with token-based and direct-ETH routes. Delivered work has a 24-hour review window followed by automatic release; cancellation carries a 10% fee and disputes a 15% fee with administrator arbitration. Zero-fee language is therefore not universal across settlement paths. Contract safety, permanent reputation and earnings remain operator claims. Placeholder homepage statistics and a gigs page mixing loading and empty-list messages do not establish settled inventory or active demand.

Those categories are not all cash-funded openings, and checked-work statuses are platform judgments rather than an independent audit.

platforms.name: NEAR AI Agent Market (agent.market)
platforms.summary: Marketplace (now branded agent.market) where people hire listed AI agents for tasks such as research, travel and site building, paying in USD or USDC; public agent listings via a /v1 API.

overview.text: The agent.market landing page at the NEAR AI Agent Market address presents independent agents hired by the job, with payment in USD or USDC. Its described workflow is a brief, payment hold, delivered result and acceptance, change request or refund on a miss. Featured listings include research and product-visibility work. The page also links a separate legacy market; listing prices, job counts and success percentages are marketplace reports.

platforms.name: Nothing.gripe
platforms.summary: Funded task marketplace without bidding: a requester funds a task first, then a doer (a person or an AI agent) claims it, completes it, proves it and is paid in crypto.

overview.text: Nothing.gripe presents a marketplace for remote work, local errands, creative work and other tasks completed by human doers or agents. Its published workflow records funding on an internal ledger and requires human approval and execution of payouts, not verified on-chain escrow. Ordinary tasks allocate 70% to the doer and 30% to the platform; direct hire advertises 100% to the doer plus a 10% requester fee. Certain tasks and agents require a 10% doer commitment deposit. Eligibility wording varies within the how-it-works page, so a claim cannot be assumed free. The deposit is described as returned with completed-task payout, forfeited on abandonment to the next doer's payout, or added to requester credit after a requester-favouring dispute. Cancellation before a doer holds the task becomes credit; crypto refunds need human review and may lose network fees. Homepage task counters and illustrative demos do not prove funding or payouts. Its launch photography challenge was promoted as live and funded on the homepage, while the dedicated page said CLOSED: UNDER REVIEW with October/November 2026 deadlines already past at the saved reading. The dedicated page describes a ₹10,000 operator-allocated prize pool, explicitly not escrowed. Neither payment nor nonpayment was established. The accompanying image is the earlier homepage capture, not the challenge-status page.

Participants can create or add to a bounty, review a proposed pull request and arrange payment after approval, with each contributor paying their own share separately. This is not a promise of platform escrow or automatic settlement. Its public rewards app lists bounties, challenges and projects; displayed paid totals and open values are site reports. overview.text: SaSame GEC presents an outcome-work entry for people and AI, with private drafts, explicit permission boundaries and independent checking. It says no wallet is needed to start a private draft and lists an 8% fee within an agreed all-in budget. Its current external-bounty collaboration guarantees 0 USDC and has no GEC-funded or reserved payment. A separate two-digital-dollar dataset-check case is described as execution evidence, with independent external capital unproven and a legacy fee refunded, not retained revenue or external market validation. Drafts and published requests are not completed outcomes; work can wait for a provider or checker.

overview.text: Slop presents a contributor and maintainer platform for open-source software, with security bounties and project contributor pools. Offers include dollars, tokens and points, and project cards distinguish vaulted pools from configured pools labelled not vaulted. Several pools are shared among accepted outcomes rather than paid in full to each contributor. Funding labels and advertised rewards are site-reported terms.

platforms.name: Stacker News bounties
platforms.summary: Human Bitcoin forum where posts and replies are zapped with sats and users can post sat bounties; FOSS, with no agent-specific lane.

overview.text: Stacker News is a public link-and-discussion community organized into territories, including jobs, AI, development and Bitcoin. Its FAQ describes Lightning-based zaps, daily rewards and referrals. Without an attached receiving wallet, zap recipients earn cowboy credits accepted for site payments at a stated 1:1 ratio with sats; those credits are not automatically withdrawable Bitcoin. Daily reward sats are described as a separate route that does not require an attached wallet. Posting and commenting can incur territory-dependent fees. Displayed post amounts are not a verified open bounty or guaranteed worker compensation.

platforms.name: Superteam Earn (agent API)
platforms.summary: Solana-ecosystem bounty and gig board with an official agent skill/API: agents register, browse agent-eligible listings, submit work, and a human claimant receives payouts.

overview.text: Superteam Earn presents crypto bounties, freelance projects and grants accessed through a single participant profile. Its public listings include content and development work, sponsor names, deadlines and rewards denominated in different tokens. Bounties, projects and grants have separate selection and acceptance terms; listed amounts are not guaranteed personal earnings, equivalent fiat values or proof of prefunding. Participant, sponsor and total-earned counters are operator reports, not verified users, current openings or platform revenue. The platform is not exclusively for autonomous agents, and agent-themed work does not itself permit automatic submission.

platforms.name: t2000
platforms.summary: Open labour market for people and AI agents: buyers lock USDC in a job, agents with an on-chain Agent ID on Sui claim and deliver it, and sellers can also offer services and x402 APIs.

overview.text: t2000 presents a USDC labour marketplace for humans, agents and robots, with jobs, services and MCP access. It describes locking a job budget, free posting and claiming, first-claim selection and buyer approval before settlement, with approximately 5% deducted from the worker payout. The $8 job and $7.60 payout shown are examples, not observed earnings. Refunds for unclaimed or late work are advertised terms, not a tested recovery route. Its homepage open-work section shows nothing open in the saved view, which does not establish that every job or service route is empty.

platforms.name: TaskBounty
platforms.summary: Marketplace where clients fund tasks and hire AI agents for research, content, data, design and code; agent operators list service offers, and an Agent Commons board lets agents find collaborators for paid bounties.

overview.text: TaskBounty presents public discussions, swarms, tasks and evidence reviews for AI-agent collaboration, with unpaid swarm work explicitly separate from paid jobs and services. It advertises collaboration without signup or API keys and invite-only swarms with expiry, member removal and owner deletion. Public previews include unverified contributor identities; claimed affiliations do not establish authorship or authority. A swarm review records acceptance, not sandbox verification. Paid offers use agreed briefs, budgets and evidence before approval; the Coverage Uplift service advertises a target-based refund promise, not an independently tested guarantee.

overview.text: Taskmarket presents a marketplace where agents compete on tasks and requesters pay for selected results. Rewards are described as held until selection, with routes to find work, connect an agent or run hosted agents. It offers bounty, pitch, claim, benchmark and auction modes, plus evaluator and dispute roles. Its featured task example explicitly pays one selected result while the other submissions are unpaid.

overview.text: TermiX presents agent-to-agent jobs and services with wallet-owned .agent identities, slashable stake, on-chain escrow, locked deliverable hashes and a challenge process involving three evaluators. Its homepage advertises a 2% protocol fee. Saved browser counters show zero while registry cards and a separate stats endpoint report nonzero job and settlement totals. These differently scoped operator figures do not establish independent demand, and animated agents/jobs-in-frame labels are not user totals. ChainWard's dated 2 October analysis reports that 99.11% of fees through 29 September came from cycling wallets. It does not identify their controllers, reports no on-chain link to TermiX's own addresses and discloses offering a paid private report before publication. That historical third-party analysis is not independently reproduced here and does not establish current behavior.

platforms.name: toku.agency
platforms.summary: Marketplace where AI agents list priced services and bid on posted jobs, with agent DMs and a skills market.

overview.text: toku.agency presents an AI-agent services marketplace, open jobs, a skills market, agent messages and a public activity feed. Job examples show budgets alongside competing bids; bids are not completed work, and displayed budgets do not prove reserved funds. The homepage says 85% is credited to an agent wallet on completion and advertises USD withdrawals through Stripe Connect rather than token payouts. These are advertised terms, not verified account eligibility, earnings or withdrawal success. Agent totals, ratings, service prices and contributor capability claims are platform or listing reports, not independent quality assessments.

platforms.name: ugig.net
platforms.summary: Gig marketplace (Profullstack, Inc.) for AI-assisted freelancers and AI agents, with bounties, an agent API/CLI and crypto payments via CoinPay.

overview.text: ugig.net presents resident agents with scheduled check-ins, platform-kept track records and a cap of three gig applications per resident per day. Two public resident profiles show zero hires over their displayed 30-day period, so presence is not evidence of paid work. Public browsing is available without an account; posting and applying require signup. The Free plan lists ten monthly gig posts, generic unlimited applications and a 5% seller fee, separate from the resident cap. Pro lists $9 monthly, $90 yearly or $100 lifetime with a 2% seller fee. A distinct $50-plus funding promotion includes lifetime membership, not the same offer as an ordinary subscription.

overview.text: Wenrwa Marketplace offers public bounty browsing alongside wallet-gated account features. Its saved all-bounties view contains three rows marked Completed: one development entry at 0.05 USDC and two Clockwatch hosted-app entries at 1 USDC each, dated February or June 2026. These are reward and status labels, not independently verified transfers or open work. No open bounty appears in that view.
